slides.title: Read it, got it… forgot it
slides.tldr: Reading alone fades within a week. To remember something, you have to keep asking yourself about it.

blocks.title: Writing in the sand
blocks.body: Write your name in the sand on a beach and the first wave wipes half of it away. Fresh learning works the same way: the brain erases what it is not using. But trace the same letters again and again and the grooves get deep enough that the waves can no longer reach them.

blocks.caption: How much you still remember after reading something once (roughly)

items.label: Right after reading
items.tip: You have just read it, so it all feels clear — and that feeling is exactly what fools you.

items.label: After 20 minutes
items.tip: Not even half an hour later, almost half of it has already gone blurry.

items.label: After 1 day
items.tip: By the next day two thirds are gone. This is the best moment to review.

items.label: After 1 week
items.tip: Without review, a week later only the rough outline of the idea is left.

blocks.body: Reading is not learning. Trying to remember is.

aside.body: After a tutorial you feel you understood everything, yet nothing comes back when you need it at work. This whole platform is designed to fix exactly that.

items.meaning: A graph of how quickly we lose what we learned as time passes.
Trying to bring the answer back from memory before you look at it.

check.q: What is the most effective way to make something stick?
check.a: Not re-reading it. Try to recall it without looking at the answer, and do that again every few days.

slides.title: The four-step learning loop
slides.tldr: See → recall → check → come back. This loop is what turns small pieces of knowledge into lasting ones.

blocks.body: Every topic here is taught in four small steps. Each step makes your brain do a different kind of work, so skipping one breaks the loop. One small step (a sub-segment) per sitting is enough — no more.

blocks.caption: Four steps to make a topic stick

steps.title: 1. See
steps.body: Understand one idea on a slide, through a picture and an example.
steps.tip: Seeing a picture and words together lets the brain store the idea in two ways. This is called dual coding.

steps.title: 2. Recall
steps.body: On a flashcard, say the answer yourself before you look.
steps.tip: The harder it is to remember, the stronger the memory gets. That is active recall.

steps.title: 3. Check
steps.body: Get quiz questions wrong and read why. Mistakes teach you the most.
steps.tip: The brain takes an explanation far more seriously when it arrives right after a wrong answer.

steps.title: 4. Come back
steps.body: Run the topic's flashcards again a few days later. The cards you forgot come first.
steps.tip: Reviewing with gaps of a few days is called spaced repetition, the best weapon against forgetting.

blocks.title: Your daily routine
items: One sub-segment at a time: 10 to 15 minutes.
Answer the "Ask yourself" question under each slide in your head before you reveal it.
Before starting something new, do one round of yesterday's flashcards.

aside.body: See → recall → check → come back. Stay stuck on the first step and nothing sticks.

items: Stop when you feel tired. Short sessions with breaks stay with you longer.
Quiz questions come in a shuffled order on purpose: mixing topics makes memories stronger (interleaving).

check.q: Which of the four steps teach you the most, and why?
check.a: "Recall" and "Check", because they make your brain work. Just looking takes no effort.

slides.title: The three rooms of the platform
slides.tldr: Lesson teaches with slides, Flashcards make you recall, and Quiz checks you.

blocks.body: The menu at the top has three rooms. Each one has a different job, but all three follow the same list of topics. So whatever you learn in one room, you can review in the room next door. There is no account to create: your reading progress and flashcard marks are saved in this browser.

blocks.caption: What happens in each room, and when to go there

cells: Slides with pictures, code and examples
rows.tip: The list on the left, the slide in the middle, extra context on the right — like a slide deck.
Cards play one after another like stories. Tap a card to flip it and see the answer.

cells: Multiple-choice questions with explanations, no time limit
rows.tip: When you get one wrong, the right-hand side explains why and which answer is right, with a link to the slide.

items: Can't remember something mid-task? Open search (Ctrl/⌘ + K) and type any word.
Every link opens in a new tab, so you can keep a slide in one tab and the quiz in another.

check.q: You forgot what an idempotency key is in the middle of a task. What is the quickest way to find it?
check.a: Open search (Ctrl/⌘ + K) and type "idempotency": it takes you straight to that slide.

slides.title: From a coffee cart to a big restaurant
slides.tldr: Code that runs fine for 10 users can break at 10,000 — not because the code was wrong, but because the pressure changed.

blocks.title: The coffee cart
blocks.body: The owner makes the coffee, takes the money and keeps every regular's tab in his head, all by himself. With 50 customers a day, that works beautifully. Now turn the cart into a 500-seat restaurant. One person, one espresso machine and a notebook in his head won't cut it anymore. Your CRUD app is that coffee cart.

blocks.caption: The same app under two kinds of pressure

columns.title: 10 users
items: Everything on one server, no fuss
Two people never press the same button at once
A short outage goes unnoticed
Even a slow query doesn't show
columns.tip: At small scale you almost never notice a problem, so the code looks flawless.

columns.title: 10,000 users
items: One server is now a risk: if it stops, everyone stops
The same seat gets sold to two people
A 5-minute outage means lost money
One slow query stalls the whole site
columns.tip: Under load, the weaknesses that were hiding all come out at the same time.

blocks.body: The code stays the same; the pressure changes. And when the pressure changes, the rules change too.

aside.title: The night of the Black Friday sale
aside.body: On the night of a Black Friday offer, a small e-commerce site suddenly got ten times its usual shoppers. There were 20 phones in stock, and 35 orders came in. The code had no bug as such. Nobody had asked what happens when two people press "Buy" at the same instant.

check.q: Why do small apps break when they grow — is the code just bad?
check.a: No. More users, more data and more simultaneous requests create situations that never occurred at small scale.

slides.title: The last ticket sold twice
slides.tldr: "Check first, then change" code goes wrong when two requests arrive together — the best-known trap in CRUD apps. The next slide fixes it.

blocks.body: The code below looks completely harmless: if the seat is free, book it. Test it alone and it works every time. But when Ryan and Kevin press the button at **the same moment**, both see "free" and both book the seat. The next slide shows the fix.

marks.tip: Both requests see "free" here, because nobody has saved anything yet.
The gap between checking and changing is where the trouble gets in.

blocks.caption: One seat, two requests — who saw what, and when

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Holds the true state of every seat.

actors.label: Kevin
actors.tip: Wants the very same seat at the very same moment.

messages.label: Yes, free
messages.tip: Ryan hasn't saved yet, so Kevin sees it as free too.

messages.label: Book it for me
messages.tip: The database doesn't object. It just keeps whichever write comes last.
Both got a "booking confirmed" message. Cue the argument at the station.

aside.body: This slide is the trap, shown on purpose. The very next slide fixes it with one conditional UPDATE. For rules that touch several rows, see the transactions and concurrency topic.
If there's a gap between checking and changing, someone else will walk through it.

check.q: The code works when tested alone, so why does it fail in production?
check.a: Alone, requests arrive one after another. In production two arrive together, and both decide based on the old state.

slides.title: Check and book in one step
slides.tldr: Move the check into the write itself: one UPDATE that only succeeds while the seat is still free, then read how many rows changed.

blocks.title: The stamp that refuses
blocks.body: At a train station ticket counter, the old way was: look at the chart, say "free", then reach for the stamp. In that gap another clerk can stamp the same seat. The new way is a stamp that refuses to print on a seat that already has ink. Ryan's stamp lands first. Kevin's finds ink, does nothing, and Kevin hears "taken" at once.

marks.tip: The check lives inside the write. The database tests "still free?" and books the seat as one step.
0 rows changed means the WHERE no longer matched: the seat was already taken.

blocks.caption: Same two requests as before, now ending with one owner

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Checks "still free?" and changes the row in one step.

actors.label: Kevin
actors.tip: Presses "Book" for seat 12 at the very same moment.

messages.label: UPDATE … WHERE seat is still free
UPDATE … WHERE seat is still free

messages.note: Row locked for Ryan; Kevin waits a moment
messages.tip: The database lets only one UPDATE touch this row at a time.

messages.label: 0 rows changed: already taken
messages.tip: Kevin's WHERE is checked after Ryan's change, and it no longer matches.

blocks.title: What it costs
items: It guards one row. If the rule spans several rows, such as a seat plus an account balance, use a transaction with a lock.
It says only "0 rows", not why. To answer "no such seat", look the seat up first.
A bulk UPDATE skips entity events and does not refresh Seat objects you already loaded.

aside.body: Don't ask, then act. Act, and let the database tell you whether it worked.

items.meaning: All-or-nothing in one indivisible step: no other request can slip in halfway.
How many rows the database actually changed. 0 means the WHERE matched nothing.

items.label: More ways to make a step atomic

check.q: Kevin's UPDATE came back with 0 rows changed. What should the controller answer?
check.a: A 409 "Seat taken". Zero rows means the WHERE no longer matched, so someone booked the seat first.

slides.title: So what is architecture?
slides.tldr: Architecture is the set of decisions that cost the most to change later.

blocks.title: The pillars and the paint
blocks.body: If you dislike the wall color, you can repaint it in one afternoon. If a pillar is in the wrong place, you have to knock the house down. Some software decisions are like paint and some are like pillars. Spotting the pillars and thinking them through up front is what architecture is.

blocks.caption: The upper layers change easily; the lower ones are the hardest to change

layers.label: Paint and furniture
layers.tip: Change them whenever you like. A long meeting about these is wasted time.

layers.label: The walls
layers.sub: Which library, how code is split
layers.tip: Changeable, but it takes effort: a few days to a few weeks of work.

layers.label: Pillars and foundation
layers.sub: Data model, service boundaries, API contract
layers.tip: Everything else stands on these. Changing them takes months and carries huge risk.

blocks.body: Not all decisions are equal. Spend your time on the ones that are hard to change.

items: Before any new decision, ask yourself: "How many days would it take to change this in six months?"
If the answer is "one afternoon", decide fast. If it's "a few months", stop, think, and ask others.
Thinking ahead has a price: you can only plan for what you know today. Keep the pillars few, and decide each as late as is safe.

items.label: Is there a door back, or not?

check.q: A variable name and a database table design: which is the architectural decision, and why?
check.a: The table design. A name changes in a minute, but changing the shape of a table full of data means touching the whole system.

slides.title: A map of the whole course
slides.tldr: A request travels from the user to the database along one path, and each topic in the course covers one stop on that path.

blocks.body: Don't worry — you don't have to learn it all at once. The picture below shows a typical system; hover over each box to see which topic teaches it. Going through the topics in order works fine, and when work demands it you can jump straight into any topic.

blocks.caption: A typical system — and which topic covers each part

nodes.label: User
nodes.tip: Where everything starts. How a Vue app talks to the API is covered in topics B and Q.

nodes.label: API
nodes.tip: The door every request comes through. API design (B) and security (J) live here.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.tip: Keeping an answer instead of building it again each time — topic D.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: Data (C), transactions (F) and money handling (K) — the biggest part of the course.

nodes.label: Queue
nodes.tip: A line that holds slow jobs such as emails and reports — topics G and L.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.tip: Picks jobs off the queue and does them in the background, so the user never waits.

edges.label: It checks the cache first — on a hit, it answers immediately
On a miss, it reads from or writes to the database
It drops the slow jobs into a queue
A worker works through them one by one, later
The user gets a fast response

blocks.title: Your path through the course
items: Start with A (ways of thinking) and B (APIs) — they lay the foundation.
Then C, D, F and G — the ones you'll use most in daily work.
The rest whenever your work calls for them.

aside.body: In front of every box, ask the same question: "What happens if this breaks?" The whole course is the answer to that one question.

items.label: The full journey of one request

check.q: Where does a slow job like sending an email go, instead of running inside the request?
check.a: Into a queue. The API responds right away, and a worker does the job in the background.
